articles.title: Terror at 10,000 Meters: What a Bumpy Flight in Argentina Taught Me About Deregulation
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
Even before we aborted our first attempted landing in the southern mountain town, I knew our flight was in trouble. High winds had been tossing our plane around like a fluttering leaf. Up and down the cabin, passengers were vomiting into the aisles.
To my left, one of my travel companions was whispering prayers to himself at an increasingly frantic pace. In the middle seat, I was thumbing through rosary beads as fast as my trembling fingers would allow. To my right, my other travel companion had a more stoic reaction. "The one time my domestic flight in Argentina leaves on time," he said, shaking his head.
The point of the trip was to take in the beauty of Bariloche, a popular lakeside tourist destination nestled in the Patagonian Andes along the Chilean border. Recent deregulation of Argentina's domestic airline market ensured it was practical and affordable to fly there from Buenos Aires, where we'd been staying since we'd arrived in the country. Weather permitting, we'd even go skiing.
Unfortunately, the weather wasn't even permitting us to land.
I am not generally a nervous flyer. The rational part of my brain reminds me of how safe air travel is in the United States, and that's usually enough to calm the reptilian jitters I feel during normal levels of turbulence. But I was not in the United States, and these were not normal levels of turbulence. Worse still, the airline we'd voluntarily opted to fly on was a budget carrier whose ability to offer our bumpy flight was made possible by the government's liberalization of the industry. For the entirety of my professional career, I had been cheering on the cause of deregulation. Now, here I was praying that a cut-rate profit-seeking carrier would keep my fellow passengers and me safe during exceptionally challenging flight conditions.
With every bounce and dip, I became more convinced that I would realize my biggest fear of dying an ironic death.
For decades, Argentina's aviation industry had been dominated by the state-owned and state-protected national carrier Aerolíneas Argentinas. The airline began life under President Juan Perón in 1950. For decades, it cruised along as an overstaffed, monopoly-protected enterprise under a variety of civilian and military regimes. In 1990, the government attempted to improve the state's balance sheet by privatizing the airline. But the carrier still suffered year after year of losses, despite continued state protection from competitors.
Renationalization in 2008 did not improve Aerolíneas Argentinas' financial situation. Instead, it made the government's fiscal situation worse. State subsidies to the renationalized airline totaled $8 billion by 2021. The state-owned carrier also developed a reputation for unreliability. While official on-time rates remained high, many travelers to Argentina are familiar with the national carrier's drastic changes to departure times, and even changes to which airport a flight was leaving from.
The privileges Aerolíneas Argentinas enjoyed in Argentina came at the cost of competing airlines and passengers generally. Between 2019 and 2022, 17 airlines ceased operations in the country. Companies such as LATAM Airlines, which tried to compete with Aerolíneas Argentinas, left in large part due to government restrictions and union conflicts. Prices were high and service quality was low.
When Javier Milei won the presidency, the airline was identified as a prime candidate for privatization.
That has not happened. But Milei's deregulation of the nation's airline industry does appear to have been beneficial for Aerolíneas Argentinas and the flying public as a whole. The airline slashed unprofitable routes and trimmed staff. In 2025, it posted its first operating profit since the 2008 nationalization.
Milei's "open skies" policy, which liberalized prices and allowed more foreign carriers to offer service between Argentine cities, saw the number of flights offered rise. In 2025, a record 50.6 million passengers flew to, from, and within Argentina.
My plane eventually landed safely, but we then had to wait an hour for our bags to be unloaded, giving me time to reflect on the policy implications of my traumatic experience. Without the lower prices and wider availability of flights created by deregulation, perhaps I would have stayed on the ground and avoided the terrifying flight altogether? Or maybe, in a more statist world, I would have paid more to a state monopoly for the same near-death experience?
The rosary that remained clutched in my still-trembling hands suggested a third possibility. Perhaps there was no policy takeaway here: Perhaps weather is just weather, and our prayers are heard under a variety of regulatory regimes.
We opted to fly a competing airline on our departure from Bariloche. I reasoned that it would be at least as safe as the carrier we flew in on. God's grace is infinite. Unlike the Argentine government, He could afford to protect more than one airline.
The post Terror at 10,000 Meters: What a Bumpy Flight in Argentina Taught Me About Deregulation appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Argentina's Oldest Café Has Outlasted Authoritarians, Bureaucrats, and Lockdowns
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
On Avenida de Mayo in Buenos Aires, a line forms each day outside a café with a green awning, gold lettering on its glass, and wooden doors. In its main hall, three wax figures sit at a marble-topped oak table: Jorge Luis Borges, Alfonsina Storni, and Carlos Gardel. In a separate room, a weekly tango show gives visitors a taste of the Buenos Aires musical experience. The Gran Café Tortoni has been in business since 1858—older than the Argentine air force, Peronism, and the Argentine peso.
Historically, Tortoni was a hub for the exchange of art and ideas and helped develop the city's artistic and literary life. It hosted many of the protagonists of Argentina's rich history, and endured the worst of its upheavals, outlasting every government that promised to save the country but brought it to its knees instead.
The café was founded by Jean Touan, a French immigrant who arrived during one of Argentina's many immigrant waves. The country was young—it had declared independence in 1816—and hungry for ambitious individuals. By the time the café moved from Calle Esmeralda to its current home in 1894, Buenos Aires had begun a stunning transformation that earned it a reputation as "the Paris of South America." Tortoni's vitreaux ceilings, oak and leather chairs, and marble sidewalk tables made the café a miniature of the French capital. Buenos Aires' belle epoque reflected the country's increasing prosperity: By 1910, it was among the richest countries in the world.
Argentina's riches weren't only economic. Its cultural and intellectual life was flourishing, and Tortoni helped sustain it. In the 1920s, artists and intellectuals would gather in cafés around the city to discuss art and ideas. One evening in 1926, a group of them (including the renowned painter Benito Quinquela Martín) took their conversations to Café Tortoni—and kept coming back. The group occupied some of the best tables but consumed very little. Wanting to support the intellectuals but also eager to make room for paying customers, Pedro Curutchet, the new owner of the café, eventually approached the group and offered the basement for their gatherings. They accepted the offer and renovated the space themselves.
Within weeks, they founded La Peña del Tortoni, a private club of painters, writers, and musicians who discussed art and ideas and held concerts, poetry readings, and exhibitions. Curutchet told the group that "here one may converse, speak, and drink with moderation, and give the measure of one's savoir faire. But only art and the spirit have the right to express themselves here without measure."
In the span of 17 years, La Peña offered Porteños a place to express themselves freely over pastries and cortados. Some of the most renowned and influential cultural figures of the time, including Nobel laureate Luigi Pirandello, poet Alfonsina Storni, writer Federico García Lorca, and tango icon Carlos Gardel, gathered around Tortoni's oak and marble tables.
By the 1940s, as the famous tertulias were dying down, Argentina had begun experiencing the political turbulence that has characterized much of its history since then. In 1943, the country suffered its second military coup. The final blow came not from the military government, however, but from the Buenos Aires municipal government: It sent La Peña a notice saying the basement failed to meet the municipality's safety standards, ordering the project to end. Its leaders decided to acquiesce instead of fighting the bureaucrats.
La Peña's demise wasn't the end of Tortoni, and the café was a haven for art and free expression during Argentina's authoritarian years. It remained a place to meet, debate, and enjoy art through successive military coups and various other governments, including the rise of Peronism. Among the personalities Tortoni hosted during the tumultuous years of 1943–1982 were the writer Jorge Luis Borges—who "exchanged verses" with fellow poet Carlos Mastronardi, according to author Laura Arias—and the renowned scientist René Favaloro, who gave a speech where La Peña used to gather.
Tragedies came and went, but Tortoni kept serving its customers. It stood firm through the 1871 yellow fever epidemic, which killed about 8 percent of Buenos Aires' population. It endured six military coups—one of them among the bloodiest in Latin American history—and operated through periods of hyperinflation. Police shot people mere feet from its doors during the 2001 riots. Through it all, Tortoni answered only to its customers, remaining a place where people could meet over coffee and enjoy cultural offerings.
President Alberto Fernández's draconian pandemic restrictions brought the place to the edge of demise. Argentina had the world's longest continuous lockdown, lasting 234 days, among other oppressive measures. The government forced Tortoni to shut down after 162 years of continuous operation—again in the name of "safety"—and it was nearly forced to close its doors forever. As restrictions eased, Tortoni bounced back wounded but undefeated.
Nowadays, Tortoni is mostly a tourist attraction. It still serves coffee and hosts cultural activities, but it has adapted to the changing demands of its customers, who now are more likely to debate through their screens than in groups gathered at a café. Tortoni's resilience mirrors that of Argentina itself: a society that has struggled through chaos and misrule but keeps managing to push forward. When the café almost closed in 2020, a waiter told an Argentine outlet: "May these 162 years last another 162."
The post Argentina's Oldest Café Has Outlasted Authoritarians, Bureaucrats, and Lockdowns appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Brickbat: Caught on Tape
articles.content:
Former Lee County, Florida, sheriff's deputy Brandon Sellers was charged with misdemeanor battery after using force against a handcuffed prisoner. Sellers pulled over and arrested a man on October 26 for street racing. He later told a supervisor he had had to use force when the driver became unruly while being processed at the station. But after noticing inconsistencies in Sellers' story, the supervisor reviewed footage from the holding cell, which showed that while the driver was handcuffed, Sellers twice grabbed him by the neck and forcefully threw him toward a chair. Sellers resigned from the department before the investigation concluded.

The post Brickbat: Caught on Tape appeared first on Reason Magazine.
